title: K-nearest neighbors
summary: Predict from the labels of nearby stored examples under a chosen distance metric.
why: Provides a nonparametric baseline with almost no model-fitting objective.
interview: Explain distance concentration and choose an index for the dimension and metric.
derivation: In many high-dimensional distributions, nearest and farthest distances become less distinguishable in relative terms. This is distribution dependent, not a theorem that all high-dimensional data are equally hard.

KD-Trees partition coordinate space and Ball Trees bound metric balls. Their pruning often degrades in high dimensions. Inverted-file indexes partition vector space into coarse clusters; sparse text inverted indexes map terms to postings.

steps.note: Fit cost is mostly storage and index construction.
steps.transformation: Save training transform, vectors, and labels

steps.note: Scaling and normalization must match the stored examples.
Brute force costs O(B*N*F); ANN trades exactness for speed.
steps.transformation: Search exact or approximate nearest neighbors

steps.note: Define ties, distance weights, and zero-distance handling.

traps: Cosine distance is undefined for a zero vector unless a convention is chosen.
Scaling features using test data leaks information.
ANN recall affects the classifier or retrieval result downstream.
tradeoff: Larger k smooths predictions and reduces variance while potentially increasing bias.
code:
from math import sqrt

def nearest(query, points, k):
    if not 1 <= k <= len(points):
        raise ValueError("k must be within the dataset size")
    distances = [(sqrt(sum((a-b)**2 for a,b in zip(query,p))), i) for i,p in enumerate(points)]
    return sorted(distances)[:k]

assert nearest([0,0], [[3,4], [1,0]], 1)[0][1] == 1

explanations.title: Distance, scaling, and the value of k
paragraphs: KNN stores training examples, retrieves the nearest k under a defined distance, then votes for classification or averages for regression. Distance-weighted predictions give closer neighbors more influence and require an exact-match policy to avoid division by zero.

Euclidean distance emphasizes large coordinate differences, Manhattan sums absolute differences, and cosine compares directions. Unit-normalized vectors make squared Euclidean distance equal 2-2*cosine, preserving neighbor ordering. Without normalization these rankings can differ.

Small k can fit noise and has higher variance. Larger k smooths predictions and can erase small minority neighborhoods. Scale features using training statistics and choose k with a split that respects correlated users or time.

explanations.title: Why neighborhoods weaken in high dimensions
paragraphs: For a centered unit sphere inside a side-two hypercube, the volume ratio is pi^(D/2)/(Gamma(D/2+1)*2^D). It shrinks rapidly with dimension. Covering a high-dimensional region with a dense local sample can therefore require enormous data.

For many common data distributions, nearest and farthest distances become closer in relative terms as dimension grows. This is distribution-dependent: low intrinsic-dimensional structure can still produce useful neighborhoods.

Irrelevant features add distance noise. Metric learning, feature selection, or a validated projection can improve neighborhoods. PCA preserves variance, which may not coincide with preserving task-relevant nearest neighbors.

explanations.title: Brute force, trees, and inverted indexes
paragraphs: Exact brute-force search costs about O(ND) per query and can be competitive with batched matrix operations. KD-Trees partition coordinate space; Ball Trees bound metric regions. Both rely on pruning that often deteriorates with dimension.

An inverted-file vector index assigns vectors to coarse clusters and probes a subset at query time. A sparse text inverted index maps terms to postings, which is a different use of the term inverted index. Approximate indexes trade recall for latency and memory.

Measure recall against exact neighbors and then evaluate downstream classification or retrieval quality. A fast index can be accurate for vector similarity but still retrieve semantically wrong examples if the embedding model or distance contract is wrong.
